Spreadsheets didn't just impact accounting, but engineering. I was working in the nuclear industry in the early '80's for one of the power plant design companies. One of the things the group I worked in did was to calculate the radioactive isotope inventory for various components, in various scenarios. This included what would be put into containment for various accident scenarios. We had programs to do that calculation, but due to the limits of computers back then, the calculations for the accident scenarios were limited to specific time slices: Immediate, 1 hour, 10 hours, 100 hours, etc. The inventory of any given radionuclide was assumed to remain constant between any given time slice. This was inaccurate, since, depending on the decay rate for any given radionuclide, it could "disappear" between any one of those time slices. Tweaking the program we used to change the time slices was not a simple operation due to the nature of the code. When our department, yes department, got it's first PC, I created a spreadsheet in Lotus123 to do these calculations. I set up a row, where one column had the decay rate, and subsequent columns had the decay calculation for a time interval that was a variable from another cell. I copied that across multiple columns, and when I had the row set up, copies the whole row down the rest of the table. I then went in and updated each row for the appropriate decay rate for any given radionuclide, and I now had a spread sheet that could do the calculation for any time itnerval of interest by simply changing the value in the appropriate cell.

My perspective towards coding in general has always been about specifying what you want computers to do in some form or another. When we write code we have to have a very very clear specification in our head of what we want the computer to do as we have to represent that in code. This has happened at increasing levels of abstraction over the years with higher level programming languages (from read bits into register ...., then do instruction .... all the way to import numpy as np) to abstractions that people build LLMs are a bit different as they allow you to create programs without having to have the full spec in your head. This is good, because a lot of the stuff we (previously) did was mostly mechanical and bad, because the LLM can fill in parts of the spec that you haven't defined in a way that you don't expect (e.g. deciding it wants to subsample training points to make a model fit go faster) If we step back and think about how languages like Python even exist which is to make them more human readable and digestible than assembly or C then we can imagine a future language that is even less tokens for us to interact with to get what we want It was an interesting take on electricity I enjoyed it!
